benchmark: Cārvāka-standard continuous master with a topic-specific Political Theory twelve-panel atlas

topics.title: Contemporary Democracy, Social Change and Development
topics.benchmark_preservation: The approved design reference, prior topic artifacts and canonical Political Theory owners remain immutable.

lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
The Contemporary-Democracy Map and Stakes
[1] Elitist democracy reduces democracy to competitive leadership choice.
v
[2] Pluralism spreads influence across organised groups, not one sovereign people.
v
[3] Participatory democracy widens citizen action beyond periodic voting.
v
[4] Deliberative democracy adds reason-giving, revisability and justification.
v
VERDICT -> Democracy in mass society needs realism and justification.
ANSWER USE -> Define each model, then name its central democratic deficit.

panels.panel_title: Core Definitions and the Chapter Spine
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Core Definitions and the Chapter Spine
[1] Marxist democracy asks whose class power the political order serves.
v
[2] Substantive democracy cannot be judged by procedure alone.
v
[3] Macpherson criticises market-style democracy as too thin and possessive.
v
[4] Socialist practice stays vulnerable on rights, opposition and open contest.
v
VERDICT -> Procedure without power analysis leaves democracy too thin.
ANSWER USE -> Pair Marxist critique with one liberty-and-opposition caveat.

panels.panel_title: Democracy Models, Thinkers and Comparative Tests
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Democracy Models, Thinkers and Comparative Tests
[1] Revolution is abrupt structural rupture; evolution is gradual cumulative change.
v
[2] Popper rejects historicist inevitability and prefers piecemeal reform.
v
[3] Social change is plural: pace, agency and normativity differ by concept.
v
[4] Progress adds moral betterment; not every change counts as progress.
v
VERDICT -> Change concepts differ by pace, agency and moral content.
ANSWER USE -> Separate revolution, evolution, development and progress first.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Revolution, Evolution, Development and Progress
[1] Development is wider than GDP because rights, welfare and capability matter.
v
[2] Market, welfare, socialist, Gandhian and sustainable paths answer it differently.
v
[3] Growth may occur while exclusion, inequality or ecological harm deepen.
v
[4] A good answer moves from definition to model comparison to verdict.
v
VERDICT -> Development is broader than output and must be compared by model.
ANSWER USE -> Move from definition to model comparison, then close on legitimacy.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Development Models Beyond GDP
[1] Coleman, Pye, Almond and Powell link development to capacity and differentiation.
v
[2] Pye's crises include identity, legitimacy and participation.
v
[3] Modernisation turns unsafe when one Western endpoint is silently assumed.
v
[4] Political development must therefore be analysed without teleology.
v
VERDICT -> Political development theory is useful only when teleology is checked.
ANSWER USE -> Name one modernisation insight and one ethnocentric danger together.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Applications, Boundaries and Revision Control
[1] Dependency critique treats underdevelopment as historically produced, not delayed.
v
[2] World-systems reasoning makes core-periphery hierarchy central.
v
[3] Kothari is a named-scholar addition, not a Gauba-page citation here.
v
[4] India-specific change must be read through diversity and institutional reach.
v
VERDICT -> Underdevelopment can be structured historically, not simply staged.
ANSWER USE -> Use India as illustration, not as proof-text for one theory.

panels.panel_title: Elite Theory, Gramsci and Competitive Leadership
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Elite Theory, Gramsci and Competitive Leadership
[1] Populism divides society into a pure people and a corrupt elite.
v
[2] Its danger lies in anti-plural exclusive representation, not anti-elitism alone.
v
[3] Popular democracy pluralises channels; populism collapses them into one voice.
v
[4] Winning elections is necessary but not sufficient for legitimacy.
v
VERDICT -> Populism is not just anti-elitism; anti-pluralism is the key risk.
ANSWER USE -> Distinguish popular democracy from populism before citing mandates.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Political Development, Modernisation and Kothari
[1] Ecological political theory is distinct from sustainable-development policy.
v
[2] Anthropocentric, biocentric and ecocentric views disagree on moral standing.
v
[3] Productivism treats output growth as the master political goal.
v
[4] Climate-development conflict needs limits, justice and democratic accountability.
v
VERDICT -> Ecology becomes political when growth, standing and justice converge.
ANSWER USE -> Keep ecological theory separate from sustainable development.

panels.panel_title: Dependency, Indian Application and Objection-Reply Chains
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Dependency, Indian Application and Objection-Reply Chains
[1] Intergenerational justice asks how present decisions answer to future persons.
v
[2] Hardin does not settle the issue because Ostrom shows durable commons governance.
v
[3] Environmental justice tracks siting, displacement and unequal voice.
v
[4] A just transition joins ecological restraint to compensation and participation.
v
VERDICT -> Climate legitimacy needs ecological limits and democratic fairness.
ANSWER USE -> Use Hardin, Ostrom and just transition as a sequence.

panels.panel_title: Directive Control, Quotation Safety and Source Discipline
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Directive Control, Quotation Safety and Source Discipline
[1] Digital democracy changes consent and representation without changing the vote.
v
[2] Targeted messaging can weaken shared informational baselines and accountability.
v
[3] The same platforms can lower the cost of organising and petitioning.
v
[4] Technology must be judged through democratic effects, not novelty alone.
v
VERDICT -> Digital mediation widens access while stressing informed consent.
ANSWER USE -> Name one democratic gain and one democratic loss before the verdict.
CENTRAL FOCUS
MCQ Remediation and Trap Repair
[1] Democratisation widens contestation, rights and accountable succession.
v
[2] Backsliding erodes competition, liberties or checks while elections continue.
v
[3] Social movements organise claims outside or across routine party channels.
v
[4] Use these bridges to name processes, not to assign unsafe country labels.
v
VERDICT -> Democratisation, backsliding and movements are distinct processes.
ANSWER USE -> Diagnose the democratic function affected before naming the process.
CENTRAL FOCUS
PYQ Ownership and Answer Practice
[1] Philosophy cross-applied PYQs stay secondarily routed here, not re-owned.
v
[2] Use them as tested bridges on democracy, development and social change.
v
[3] Topic 23 original practice must remain original while preserving ownership.
v
[4] Answers should move from thesis to distinction, mechanism and graded verdict.
v
VERDICT -> Tested bridges may be used, but ownership discipline remains explicit.
ANSWER USE -> Mark Philosophy PYQs as secondary and keep Topic 23 practice original.
